_comment: Voiceover for docs/Demo-Script-Two-Cut.md, restructured 2026-08-29.
THE SHAPE CHANGED, and this is the important part. The first version narrated while the capture
browsed -- it moved between pages and held, so the words described features nobody was using.
That reads as a tour rather than a demonstration, and no amount of timing precision fixes it.
Every beat is now a PAIR: a short line naming what the feature is, then a longer one spoken
while it is actually performed on screen. The capture drives the app for real -- uploads the
spreadsheet, generates the coupon, moves the card -- so the narration has something to describe.
Kept as separate `-intro` and `-do` beats rather than one block, because the intro is spoken
over a still screen and the action beat has to start exactly when the click does. One block
would put the words for the action over the seconds before it.
EVERY CLAIM CHECKED. Not said here: that Instagram publishing exists (no publish method; the
live Meta token lacks instagram_content_publish), that payouts move money (ManualPayoutProvider
records a payment made out-of-band), or that the revenue is live (the orders are seeded).
A stock voice rather than a clone: this is workflow narration, not personality, and a
clone would be a licensing question for a fifteen-second gain.
JESSICA, not Rachel. Rachel is the default B2B pick and reads as competent and cool --
which is the wrong register for a video whose opening beat is somebody's daily frustration.
Jessica is labelled 'playful, bright, warm' and sounds like a person talking to you rather
than a narrator presenting at you. Liam ('social media creator') and Laura ('quirky') were
the other two auditioned; samples for all three are in tests/e2e/voice-samples/.
Style raised again to 0.4 with the voice change. Jessica carries warmth on her own, so this
is for emphasis across the intro/do pairs -- the -intro beats name a feature and the -do
beats narrate it happening, and a flat read makes those two register the same.
Still short of advertising warmth. A demo that sounds like an ad invites exactly the
scepticism the spreadsheet opening is designed to disarm.

beats.text: This is Tejdux. It's for brands who work with creators — and right now, are running the whole thing out of a spreadsheet. Let me show you what the free tier gives you, and then actually use each piece.
First, the free tier. One brand, twenty-five creators, one seat. No card, and no trial clock counting down.
Signing up is a name, an email, a password. That's the whole thing — and you land in a working workspace, not an onboarding queue.
Now the spreadsheet. Everyone has one: inconsistent headers, a notes column doing four jobs, someone's initials in a cell.

Drop it straight in. It reads the columns and works out which are creators, which are handles, which are fees — and then it shows you what it found, before it commits to anything. You check it, and the roster is in.
Next, the bit a spreadsheet genuinely cannot do. When a sale arrives, which creator earned it?
Give each creator their own code. Generate them per creator, in one pass — and from here every order placed with one is attributed to the person whose code it was, automatically.
Campaigns get a board. But not a tracker you keep in sync by hand.
Move a card and the page behind it moves. Move the page and the card follows. One truth, two views — and nothing to reconcile on a Friday afternoon.
Then the campaign page itself. Describe what you're selling, and you get a page rather than a blank canvas.

Pick the shape, write the words, and watch the real page build as you type. Then drop the creator's coupon straight into it — the code they were given, on the page their audience lands on. Rewrite every line if you want; you can't break the layout, because nothing in here sets a colour or a position. Publish, and the link is live with the tracking already wired in.
And it all lands here. What each creator brought in, what they're owed, and what you've already paid them. No guessing at the end of the month.

That's the free tier — all of it. Paid adds more creators, your whole team, and several brands if you're an agency. Coming next: handing a page to a creator to write in their own voice, and a share kit that sizes the post for them.
